newsitem.title: BOSNIA: Rival Bosnian Serb factions vie for police power.
newsitem.headline: Rival Bosnian Serb factions vie for police power.

text.p: Supporters of Bosnian Serb President Biljana Plavsic rallied on Tuesday against hardliners who refuse to relinquish control of police forces in the northern town of Banja Luka.
"Don't give your town to tyrants. We want freedom," Plavsic told a crowd of several thousand in pouring rain.
Plavsic and her political rivals -- who are loyal to ex-president and indicted war criminal Radovan Karadzic -- are vying for control of police forces in Banja Luka.
Plavsic has announced new chiefs for the town's police and state security office but her opponents running the Bosnian Serb interior ministry have ignored her appointments.
Her newly-appointed police chief, Milan Sutilovic, was detained on Tuesday morning by state security agents who demanded he resign. Sutilovic refused and was later released.
Plavsic's special police seized control of the main Banja Luka police station on Sunday because they said the building was being used to tap the president's telephones.
The special police units withdrew on Monday evening after NATO troops were deployed around the building to prevent a possible clash between rival groups of police.

Plavsic called on her supporters to stage daily demonstrations on the same spot until her police forces had regained control of the police station, which Karadzic loyalists reoccupied on Monday night.
"That building (pointing to the police station) has to be cleared and filled with honourable policemen," she said.
The interior ministry, run by Karadzic loyalist Dragan Kijac, issued a statement saying it would refuse to recognise her appointments in Banja Luka, the largest town in Bosnia's Serb territory.
"According to the constitution, appointments and personnel policy in the field of security is exclusively under the authorisation of the interior minister," the statement said.
The interior ministry said Plavsic violated the constitution and that her decision was "illegal".
The conflict between Plavsic and Karadzic's allies erupted in June when she called for the suspension of the interior minister and accused him of tolerating large-scale corruption.

Plavsic appeared at the rally after two hours of crisis talks with U.S. envoy Robert Gelbard, the international High Representative to Bosnia, Carlos Westendorp, and the commander of the NATO-led peace force, U.S. General Eric Shinseki.

In a setback for Karadzic's allies, the Bosnian Serb Minister of Finance Ranko Travar submitted his letter of resignation on Tuesday saying he could no longer take part in trying to resolve the conflict.
Several senior members of Karadzic's ruling party in Banja Luka resigned over the weekend.
